title: US and Denmark Reach Greenland Security Deal After Trump's Threats
summary:
The US and Denmark have announced a deal on Greenland's security, resolving a diplomatic dispute that began when President Donald Trump threatened to seize the semi-autonomous Danish territory by force.

Greenland is a massive Arctic island that belongs to Denmark but governs itself. Trump argued it was strategically vital for defense and rich in minerals. His repeated demands to "take" Greenland earlier this year prompted protests in Greenland's capital, Nuuk, and outcry from Denmark and other Nato members.

Under the new deal, Trump said Denmark would grant the US "permanent control over security, and all other needs" in Greenland. In a post on Truth Social, he said the deal came with "no cost to the United States" and included a rule that no US adversary could maintain a military presence or "make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval."

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen welcomed the agreement in a joint statement. They said it "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" while recognizing "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination." That means Greenlanders get to decide their own future.

Nato said it welcomed the deal, which would "help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region." French President Emmanuel Macron said it helped "reaffirm Danish sovereignty" and that "international law is respected."

No text of the agreement has been released. It is expected to be signed at the UN General Assembly next week, but it would still need to go through parliamentary procedures to take effect. Some Danish media interpreted the outcome as a quiet diplomatic win for Denmark. One headline in the newspaper Berlingske read: "Don't tell Trump that it's the Kingdom of Denmark that has won."
why_it_matters: The deal shows how much Arctic power politics now shapes relations between allies: a dispute that started with a threat to take territory by force ended in a negotiated text that both sides can call a win. It is also a live lesson in how sovereignty, self-determination and alliance bargaining actually work — much of it happening in paragraphs the public never gets to read.

keywords.explanation: Governing itself in most everyday matters while still being part of a larger country.
A country's or a people's right to govern themselves without outside control.
The principle that a country's land and borders must not be taken or changed by force.
The right of a group of people to decide their own political future.
Relating to a parliament — the group of elected politicians who make a country's laws.

background_read: Greenland is the world's largest island, sitting between the Arctic and Atlantic oceans on the shortest missile and shipping routes between North America and Europe, which is why major powers watch it closely. It is part of the Kingdom of Denmark but has run its own internal affairs since home rule in 1979, and its capital is Nuuk (a small city of roughly 20,000 people).

The United States has kept a military base in northern Greenland since World War II — today called Pituffik Space Base — used for early-warning radar and space tracking. In 2019, during his first term, President Donald Trump (the US president again since 2025) suggested the United States should buy Greenland, an idea Danish leaders rejected outright.

Nato (the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, a military alliance of more than 30 mostly European and North American countries) treats Arctic security as a shared problem, which is why its reaction to the deal mattered. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen (Denmark's leader since 2019) and Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen spoke jointly, and French President Emmanuel Macron (France's president since 2017) also weighed in.

The phrases at stake have long histories: 'sovereignty' means a state's authority over its own territory, and 'territorial integrity' is the rule, written into the UN Charter, that borders must not be changed by force. 'Self-determination' is the separate idea that a people — such as Greenlanders — may decide their own political future, which is why Denmark and Greenland insisted it appear in the statement.

perspectives.description: The United States gets the security guarantees and limits on rival influence it wanted without buying or seizing the island, and it keeps a Nato ally onside instead of alienating it. Denmark and Greenland, meanwhile, avoided a confrontation and can point to written recognition of their sovereignty, which is why both governments welcomed the outcome.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — whose control, and whose consent?
perspectives.description: The phrase 'permanent control over security, and all other needs' is broad and, with no published text, hard to check. Trump's earlier threats alarmed allies and triggered protests in Nuuk, so Greenlanders may reasonably ask how much say they had in the terms and whether 'security' could quietly expand into other areas of island life.

perspectives.perspective: Analytical — the Arctic as a long-running stage
perspectives.description: Arctic security has been a shared Western project since World War II, when the US built a base in northern Greenland to watch the shortest route between North America and Russia. The language of sovereignty and self-determination lets each side claim victory while leaving unresolved who decides what happens on the island — a familiar pattern in great-power deals over small territories.

Because no text has been published and the agreement still requires parliamentary approval, what 'permanent' means in practice is undefined. The next tests are whether Greenland's self-government and Denmark's parliament accept the terms, whether other Arctic states ask for similar arrangements, and whether a future US administration treats the deal as binding.
